content:
The SF LEAN Meetup took up the task of autoformalizing the classification of surfaces as a group project. This was primarily a learning exercise rather than a test of capabilities. The majority of the work was done by agents coordinated by myself and @Jack McCarthy . We believe this is the first formalization of this classic theorem, which was posed as a lean-eval problem by @Junyan Xu .

Note the statement requires that each surface is homeomorphic to a normal form, but does not require a proof that normal forms are non-homeomorphic. This project did incorporate homology or the Euler characteristic.

Originally we planned, with AI assistance, to make a companion to Munkres "Topology", akin to Tao's companion for "Real Analysis". But since one of the gems of that book is classification of surfaces, we first focused on this.

Proof Strategy

The textbook proof is "triangulate the surface, cut it into a polygon, normalize the edge word". For formalization this needed to be translated into a certified chain of explicit homeomorphisms begining with an arbitrary C^0 manifold.

The hardest topological fact is Rado's triangulation theorem and most accounts including Munkres skip it. To my knowledge, this project also includes the first full formalization of triangulation.

One key use of LLM's was to evaluate various proofs for their amenability to formalization. In fact, if there is one notable thing about this project it is the decision to follow Edwin Moise's "Geometric Topology in Dimensions 2 and 3". The proof is longer on paper than other standard proofs but its more combinatorial and algorithmic in flavor. It uses on polygonal approximation and induction over charts. So there is a finite piecewise linear (PL) complex at each stage, the extension is one cell or chart at a time, and the termination is supplied by compactness and finite combinatorics. It only requires a polygonal version of the Jordan Curve Theorem and the Schoenflies theorem. Other standard proofs commonly use phrases like "move a curve slightly" or "thicken this arc" or "arrange that the intersections are transverse" which are intuitive but hard to formalize.

One challenge was integrating boundaries. A missing theorem from mathlib is that points on boundaries are preserved by homeomorphisms (the C^1 version of the theorem is available), and this needed to be supplied. Moise primarily treated the case of manifolds without boundaries, so the agent needed to generalize arguments to accommodate manifolds with boundary. At times the agent seemed to be flailing, playing "whack-a-mole" as generalizing the argument in one place revealed shortcomings in another. I asked it to finish the proof end-to-end for manifolds without boundary, then to go back, and it made faster progress. With hindsight, a better approach would have been to use the trick where a suface with boundary can be doubled to give a surface without boundary.

After triangulation, the rest of the proof followed Gallier & Xu's "A Guide to the Classification Theorem for Surfaces", which was included as a reference on the lean eval statement. The standard normal form argument focuses on the manipulation of cyclic words, but the formal proof must certify that each rewrite induces a homeomorphism between the quotient spaces.

The final proof has ~90k loc establish triangulation, with supporting topological basics about C^0 manifolds and infrastructure for manipulating PL complexes. Another ~50k loc handle the combinatorial presentation, it's realization by quotienting, and the process of normalization. It was completed mostly using GPT 5.6 Sol-xhigh in about 60 hours, with some assist from Claude Fable and weaker versions

Working with agents

At one point, the agent claimed a proof of triangulation. But when it was audited with newer model, substantial flaws were uncovered. I was pushing the model to finish, I got the impression the model was like an over-eager student, wanting to put the best foot forward, minimizing shortcomings. Later I emphasized going step-by-step bottom-up got better results. The standard advice is "make sure the definitions are and theorem statements are correct". This is more challenging to verify for a proof in a partly finished state, where intermediate objects were misformalized.

Originally I intended to coordinate work via the in-repo lean blueprint and coordination documents, but these were not always updated by agents and became stale. The agents were much better at coordinating by carving out and claiming work via github issues. At one point, the agent was announced it dispatched 12 out of 13 sorries in the path to triangulation. However, proving the final sorry took as much time as the previous 12. The last step was genuinely hard, but I can't help but think difficult work was deferred to the end in the name of closing out goals.

Previous Formalization Work and Discussion

A zulip thread in 2024 discussed formalizing the final part of the proof: manipulating cyclic words to a normal form. Junyan Xu pointed out this was done by Dehlinger and Duford in Coq.

@Kevin Buzzard inquired about the role of diagrams in formalized proofs. This work provides a partial answer. The FiniteCyclicPresentation is a data structure which stores the darts (oriented half-edges) of a cell complex along with symmetries (such as inverting dart directions). It can be viewed as a formalization-legible representation of the properties which are visually obvious. Different formalization projects in planar topolgy have converged on a similar data structure of darts with symmetries, suggesting it's a natural representation. The thread references Dufourd's "Formalizing Generalized Maps" which uses gmaps. Hypermaps are used Gonthier's proof of the four color theorem, as well as Puitg and Dufourd's proofs of the Euler formula and a discrete Jordan curve theorem (see also the Coq package coq-jordan-curve-theorem).

There's an even older thread from 2021, which is interesting to revisit in light of advances in mathlib and autoformalization. Daniel Busch proposes tackling this theorem as a fun formalization project for an undergrad. Much of the discussion focused on smooth manifolds and a proof via Morse theory, partly because at the time topological manifolds did not exist in mathlib.

@Patrick Massot said:

The classification of surfaces is a very interesting formalization topic. I think it maximizes the amount of pain compared to the understanding you gain. I decided long ago that doing it would be both absolutely amazing and completely counter-productive when it comes to proving that formalized mathematics could be useful.

Patrick was entirely correct. A human formalization at 140k lines would have been an enormous amount of work, and would have been a bit of a curiosity. Current tools have completely changed the economics of formalization.

Follow ons

The full Shoenflies theorem was the next chapter of Edwin Moise book after triangulation, so I asked my agent to formalize that to close out an additional lean-eval challenge. Even though that many prerequisites from the text were already formalized, the theorem required an additional 60k loc. This leads credence to the decision to base triangulaion on Moise rather than a book which used on full Schoenflies to prove triangulation.

The repo now contains a fully self-contained Jordan Curve Theorem (borrowed from a different lean-eval), Schoenflies theorem, a working PL-topology toolkit, an implementation of something akin to hypermaps and Rado's triangulation theorem. Plausibly this is the most complete planar topology toolkit yet assembled, and, combined with the Euler characteristic could serve as a Tau Ceti roadmap. Alternatively this could be integrated into the GeometricTopology roadmap, whose Layer 11 touches on many of the same topics.

Another goal is to contribute this project to Vasily Ilin's lean pool project. However, the code quality is currently far below the standard required by that project.

All in all, this was a fun project, a good learning exercise about agents, LEAN and topology

Hi Ryan,

Thanks for this write-up. This was a fun project to work on. I loved collaborating with the SF Lean people. I hope in the future that groups like SF Lean, Lean NYC, Madlean (cc @Enrique Diaz Blanco), and Kevin's LLL can collaborate on more endeavors like this.

If you're anything like me, you've probably heard the statement of the classification of surfaces in a topology class, but never seen the full-proof. Certainly, I've never seen a rigorous derivation of triangulation--not even in graduate-level textbooks.

Since many mathematicians have been raising awareness about the importance of proof digestion, I think this may be a good opportunity to pause and reflect on why the Classification of Surfaces is true. In the following week, I hope to write a short report explaining the exact path that AI took to arrive at the formal proof, using visual aides to make it accessible to undergrads with only a point-set topology background.

Very nice project! I think it illustrates something that we're likely to see more of in the near future, which is that, especially in areas such as low-dimensional topology, the easiest proof to formalize is not necessarily the most conceptually appealing. Gallier & Xu discuss Conway's ZIP proof in some detail, saying that "it is well suited for a professional topologist who will know how to fill in missing technical details, but not so well for a non-expert in topology, who may even be mystified by some of the slick tricks." As you might expect, Conway's ZIP proof is probably not the best choice for a formalization project.

Anyway, my point is that we should be aware that one of the unintentional side effects of the increasing formalization of math may be a tendency to gravitate toward a single proof of a theorem, even though much of the beauty of math lies in the existence of multiple proofs of important results. Especially in certain areas, the easiest proof to formalize may not even be among the top three proofs from an aesthetic point of view.

Woah, I was not aware of Conway's ZIP proof, this is genius.

I agree that there is currently a disconnect between aesthetically pleasing proofs and formalizable proofs. This is an issue that many, such as Tao, have raised. Possible solutions include:

  • Intermediate representations (especially visual/diagrammatic reps) between Lean and informal text, capturing conceptual semantic info.
  • More tactics/metaprogramming, allowing one to skip technical details in these more "intuitive" proofs.
